Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 6Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 6 15-06-2022 23:14:3015-06-2022 23:14:30 7 So what’s this book about, anyway? I’m an aficionado of video game history, as I’ve experienced much of the evolution of the medium first hand. I also love learning new things about my favourite pastime. I became rather frustrated, though, at so many video game facts that I found, both online and in print media, that would be a simple quick-fire one or two sentence description, then fact over, move onto the next one. I had a craving for more than that: I wanted details! I didn’t just want to know that an event happened, I had a desire to learn exactly why it happened. What were the situations surrounding it, why were decisions made, what happened after a product launched, why was a feature so notable? Not many sources actually elaborated on all the specifics I hankered for. I wanted knowledge of the types of things that might not be commonly appreciated, down to the nitty-gritty details. I thought, surely I can’t be the only one thinking like this? As kind of a testbed, I wrote a series of three articles on a popular gaming website in the style I was envisaging, detailing a number of perhaps less commonly known facts about some older but well known consoles. The articles attracted overall very positive feedback from readers and I discovered… yes… there’s a void here. There’s a demographic of gamers out there that thirst for the same knowledge that I do. So, I took it upon myself to fix that problem. Using those articles as a base, I expanded upon the concept, conducted countless hours of research, and this book was finally born. If you’re like me and you love video game related trivia, but also want to learn about the fine points behind said trivia, then this book is for you! How the book is structured I’ve split the book into ‘chapters’, each based around a specific console, containing a number of detailed facts regarding that system. Each console section, or chapter, begins with a brief overview of the particular system to provide a bit of background before I launch into a number of detailed facts for it. My goal here is not to cover every single console ever made, but rather to just cover the most popular ones in this fashion – the consoles that had the greatest impact on the industry. While I’d love to elaborate more on products like the Amiga CD32, Funtech Super A’Can, Apple Bandai Pippin or Mattel Hyperscan, it’s not the purpose of this particular book. I wanted to focus on the popular consoles that you knew about when you were growing up, the devices that make you smile and point and say ‘Ah yeah! I remember that! I/we/my brother/my sister/ my neighbour/my cousin/my mate from school had one of those! It was awesome!’ I’ve also included the ones that had substantial influence on the industry even if they were not particularly successful at the time. I mention many of the others in passing if I need to make a comparison, but a full investigation into the more obscure devices in video game history wasn’t my goal with this work. This book also doesn’t cover portable gaming systems, arcade games or personal computers, focusing purely on game consoles. I’ve made it a point to make this book as easy to read as I could, explaining some often technical details in a style that makes it accessible to a wide audience. I try to steer clear of using technical jargon too much (at least not without explaining what it means), and try not to dive too deep into technical details that really aren’t too relevant for the case I’m trying to put forward. Acknowledgements Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 9Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 9 15-06-2022 23:14:3015-06-2022 23:14:30 10 CHAPTER 1 Magnavox Odyssey Launch year: 1972 (NA); 1973/1974 (EU); 1974 (Japan) M any gamers who know their history would be familiar with the name ‘Magnavox Odyssey’, at the very least. This system, created by the man many consider to be the father of video games, Ralph Baer, was released by Magnavox in 1972 – three years before even Atari’s dedicated Pong consoles. It’s recognised as the world’s first home video game console. The actual concept was first envisioned in 1966 and Baer and his small team went through a number of prototypes dubbed the ‘Brown Box’ between 1967 and 1969. They then pitched the idea to various manufacturers until Magnavox agreed to partner with them (after being approached multiple times) in 1971. Even though the console itself was discontinued only three years later in 1975, it spawned a series of dedicated systems using the Odyssey name from 1975–1977, as well as a true successor, called the Odyssey², in 1978/1979. It was unsuccessful at retail, only selling around 350,000 units. This was due to the fact it was only sold in Magnavox stores and reportedly customers were told it would only work on Magnavox televisions, which was untrue. Nevertheless, it proved that television sets could be used for more than just passively watching images and got the ball rolling on an entire industry. It had no real computing ability The Odyssey was a very simple machine, designed from the beginning to be affordable. It may sound weird, but it didn’t actually have any computing ability at all – it did not contain a processor or memory and did not possess any kind of ability to perform calculations. It couldn’t even keep a player’s score and had no way of enforcing game rules. For example, a player could move their paddle in Table Tennis to the other side of the screen if they wanted to and the player needed to penalise themselves if they veered off the track in a racing game such as Wipeout. It had no sound capability and no method of producing colour. It could display four separate Magnavox Odyssey. (Wikimedia Commons public domain [Evan-Amos]) Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 10Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 10 15-06-2022 23:14:3315-06-2022 23:14:33 M A GNAV O X O D y SSE y 11 Its game cards were not programmable While the Odyssey was indeed the first console to have interchangeable games, that’s actually a little misleading, as it didn’t work as some may have expected. Rather than being programmable ROMs, the Odyssey’s games were instead uncomplicated printed circuit boards that didn’t contain any code for the games themselves. These boards, called game cards or circuit cards, simply altered the video output signal of the system by modifying the diode logic circuits to change what was shown on the television screen. The system was fully capable of displaying all elements needed for the games itself (two ‘paddles’, a ‘ball’ and a line) and the game cards were basically just a set of jumpers that enabled the desired game. The Odyssey’s graphical capabilities were primitive, only being able to display three dots and a line that were basically light signals on the screen at once. The system included coloured transparent overlays that were designed to be temporarily stuck to the TV screen instead of having real background graphics and different games could be played on the same game card by swapping the overlay. A degree of imagination was needed to see the dots on the screen as racing cars or animals. Truth be told, the ‘video game’ aspect of the device was probably more intended as a supplementary feature rather than the main focus, because the Odyssey package also included dice, game boards, poker chips, paper money, card decks and other features of more traditional board games. images on the screen  – three dots and a line… and… that’s it. The system even used six C-size batteries as standard, though could also run off a power outlet with a separate AC power supply. It was as basic as you could possibly get – in fact the internals of the system more or less just consisted of an electronic circuit made from a series of transistors and diodes. It barely qualifies as a console, really! The system also didn’t have a physical power switch, instead powering on when a game card was inserted (so you’d need to remember to take the game card out when you were done, lest you drain the batteries). The game cards themselves more or less just altered how the internal diodes connected, but more on that a little later. The controllers were also pretty basic and consisted of three dials: one to control horizontal movement, one to control vertical movement and one that was oddly named ‘English’. English is an old term meaning to put spin on a ball and this dial controlled the vertical position of the ‘ball’, or ball equivalent. It also had one button, labelled ‘Reset’, that didn’t actually reset the game itself, but instead reset individual elements that were determined separately for each game. For example, in the Pong-type games, it returned the ball back to centre after a player had missed it and it had gone off screen, as the system was incapable of doing this automatically itself. Odyssey box, GameFAQs. (_0blivion_ / Llamaman2) Odyssey game card. (Wikimedia Commons public domain [Evan-Amos]) Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 11Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 11 15-06-2022 23:14:3315-06-2022 23:14:33 SECRETS OF VIDEO GAME C ONSOLES 12 and Table Tennis, so much so that he took the idea back to his newly formed Atari company. He was more focused on creating a driving game at the time, though, so he asked one of his newly recruited young engineers, Allan Alcorn, to create a clone, although reportedly didn’t inform Alcorn that he had taken the idea from the Odyssey. In fact, Bushnell had no real intention of releasing it as a commercial product (he considered the action of hitting a ball back and forth a bit too simplistic), so was treating it as a straightforward training exercise for the inexperienced Alcorn. Alcorn, however, jumped These inclusions, for the record, were entirely of Magnavox’s doing – Ralph Baer did not approve of them. Indeed, many of the ‘video games’ were designed to be played alongside the non- electronic aspects. That being said, the Odyssey did interestingly feature the first video game light gun (that actually looked like a bona fide rifle) as a separate accessory. Instead of having a title, each game card was simply numbered, though the games that each card could play had individual names. Twenty- eight games in total, contained on eleven game cards, were released for the system (around half of which were included in the box). The final card was labelled ‘12’ rather than ‘11’ (it seemed that card ‘11’ was skipped as the game planned for it was included on card ‘8’ instead). Many of them were simple target shooting games or variations of a game that would be later known as Pong, which segues nicely into the next fact… Atari copied the idea of Pong from the Odyssey While the Odyssey wasn’t particularly successful, it caught the eye of Nolan Bushnell, the creator of the first commercial arcade game Computer Space and the founder of Atari. In particular, Bushnell enjoyed Odyssey games such as Volleyball, Handball, Soccer Odyssey accessories. (Wikimedia Commons public domain [Evan-Amos]) Table Tennis (Magnavox). (MobyGames [Nélio]) Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 12Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 12 15-06-2022 23:14:3415-06-2022 23:14:34 M A GNAV O X O D y SSE y 13 more than US$100 million in court up until the mid-‘90s, not including the fees and royalties they were receiving from licensing. It spawned a series of Odyssey- branded machines Even though the Odyssey itself was discontinued in 1975, it left behind a legacy, as a series of dedicated consoles followed in its footsteps, all carrying the Odyssey branding. While these only played a handful of built- in games (initially two, but later models had as many as six) and didn’t have any way to swap new games in, they were a step up from the original Odyssey on a technical level. They used internal chips, had sound capabilities, difficulty selectors and eventually became capable of on- screen scorekeeping and colour graphics. These devices primarily competed with Atari’s Pong home systems as well as other products such as the Coleco Telstar and Nintendo’s Color TV-Game product line. The first was the Odyssey 100, released in 1975. This had two games – Tennis and Hockey. Later that same year, the Odyssey 200 hit the market. This was kind of like a ‘special edition’ version of the 100, featuring an extra game called Smash (based on the real life sport of Squash), as well as support for up to four players instead of just two. The Odyssey 300 followed in 1976 and featured the same three games as the 200, but finally added on-screen digital scoring and a difficulty selector. The Pong-like games also actually functioned more like Pong, with the ball travelling at automatic angles and players only being able to move their paddles up and down. The Odyssey 400, also released in 1976, was actually something of a downgrade from the 300; it was just a slightly updated 200 really  – it played the same three into the project with both feet and made subtle improvements to the game including being able to hit the ball at different angles. When Bushnell saw this, he delayed his plans for the driving game to push it forward. This project would become Atari’s first game, Pong, released in arcades and then as dedicated home systems. The arcade games were apparently so popular that machines stopped working due to the amount of coins that had been put into them. Pong obviously revolutionised the video game industry as a whole, inspiring countless clones of its own over the years, including clone home devices. At first, Baer didn’t mind too much, as the success of Pong was helping to drive sales of the Odyssey, although he was a little annoyed that the only games people seemed to be playing were the Pong-like titles. He said: ‘Everybody played Ping-Pong and that’s it. It was a good game but what made it really popular was Pong. That’s when we realised “hell, all we had to do was stop after game number six”.’ However, Magnavox and its parent company, Sanders Associates, eventually sought to sue Atari for patent infringement, but hesitated as they weren’t sure if Atari – who were still a young company at the time – actually had enough money to pay… and they were right. If the case had gone to court, the legal costs would have exceeded Atari’s funds. Instead, the case was settled out of court, with Bushnell agreeing to pay a one-off fee of US$700,000 to Magnavox for a license to continue to produce the game. Another condition of the settlement was that Atari would hand over the rights to any consumer products they released in the next calendar year, but Atari effectively circumvented this by just waiting until the twelve months had elapsed before putting the products they had been working on to market. Magnavox and Baer wouldn’t stop at Atari and would continue to successfully win legal cases against many other companies creating Pong clones and consoles in general, including Williams, Bally Midway, Allied Leisure, Nutting Associates, Mattel, Coleco, Activision and even Nintendo. It was very lucrative for them – in total they won Odyssey 2000. (Wikimedia Commons public domain [Evan-Amos]) Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 13Secrets_of_Video_Game_Consoles_Final.indd 13 15-06-2022 23:14:3415-06-2022 23:14:34 SECRETS OF VIDEO GAME C ONSOLES 14 Three new systems were released in 1977: the Odyssey 2000, 3000 and 4000. While the 2000 and 3000 were more or less just updated Odyssey 300s, they did add a few features such as practice modes, detachable controllers and new case designs. The Odyssey 4000, however, was a top end model, adding Basketball and Gridball to the four games included on the 500 to bring the total number of games to six. In most cases, the distance the player could see was limited, because the system could only render so much on screen before it would start to negatively affect performance. While it’s difficult to say with 100 per cent certainty, Spyro the Dragon, released for the PlayStation in 1998, was more than likely the first game to solve this problem by using a system called Level-Of-Detail, or LOD. How it worked was that game objects basically had different versions of varying quality. If the player was close, the object would be rendered in the highest quality possible, but the further away the player was, the less detailed it would become.
